1:
Whether Elihu has quoted Job fairly is the first question, and most of the commentary says he has not. Clarke is blunt: my righteousness is more than God's would indeed be a blasphemous saying, but Job never said it, neither directly nor constructively. He would rather render the Hebrew I am righteous before God, taking Job's meaning to be that whatever he was in his friends' sight he knew himself righteous in God's; and Job had a right to that character, Clarke adds, because God himself had given it to him. Ellicott agrees that here again there was a misrepresentation. Job did not mean that he was none the better for being righteous, having said let mine enemy be as the wicked; what was true is only that he had said his righteousness had not delivered him from suffering. Delitzsch recasts the charge as one ponderous construction whose two questions are co-ordinate, so that the complaint is not self-comparison but non-requital: Job sets his righteousness above the divine because God makes no distinction between righteousness and sin and leaves the former unrewarded.

Henry is the one voice who thinks the first count substantially just. When Job insisted so much on his own integrity and on the severity of God's dealings, he did in effect say it, as though his services had been paid less and his sins punished more than they deserved, so that on a balanced account God would be brought in debtor to him. But Henry will not have the second count, the complaint that there is no profit in being cleansed from sin. Job had himself put those words in the mouth of prospering sinners and immediately disclaimed them, and it is not a fair way of disputing, Henry says, to charge men with those consequences of their opinions which they expressly renounce. Gill alone lets the whole charge stand, granting that Job had not said it in so many words but holding it fairly inferred from what he had said. He does draw the distinction the complaint blurs: a man's righteousness is of no advantage as to justification or title to happiness, but of great advantage otherwise, as a defence against calumny, as what makes him respectable where a vicious course is scandalous, and as the standing pleasure of a good conscience.

On the argument itself there is no quarrel. Clarke takes the bare sight of the heavens as enough to show God infinitely beyond us in wisdom and excellence, and reads the clouds as shechakim, the ethers of the Vulgate, from a root meaning to contend: the agitated and conflicting air and light whose motion produces both light and heat. Henry turns the same verse devotionally: God made man erect and bade him look up to heaven, and where idolaters looked up and worshipped the hosts of heaven we must look up and worship the Lord of those hosts. Clarke renders the conclusion literally, to a man like thyself is thy wickedness and to the son of man thy righteousness, so that one may injure or benefit oneself and others but God can neither be hurt nor profited. Henry calls the malice of sinners an impotent malice which cannot dethrone God or disturb his peace or defeat his counsels, and sets against Job's reckoning the challenge no man can take up: who has first given to God, that it might be recompensed to him? Gill enters the one qualification, that since sin is harmful to others God resents it and punishes for it, though it cannot harm him. Ellicott enters the sharper one. Elihu is here saying very much what Eliphaz and Bildad had said before him; and while it is indeed true that God is too high to be affected by man's righteousness or unrighteousness, it does not follow that he is indifferent, for then he would not be a righteous judge.
9:
The complaint behind this passage is the hardest Job had made, and Henry states it without softening: the oppressed cry out under the arm of the mighty and God does not appear to right them, which is what Job knew not how to reconcile with the justice of God and his government. Is there a righteous God, Henry asks for him, and can it be that he should so slowly hear, so slowly see? Elihu's answer, as Henry reads it, is that if the cries are not heard the fault is not in God but in the cries. They are complaining cries, wailing cries, the cry of nature and passion rather than of grace, and they have not cried unto God with their heart though they howled upon their beds. Clarke says the same in a clause he repeats like a refrain: they bewail their calamities but do not sorrow for the cause of them, they cry against their oppressors but they call not upon God. Ellicott puts a different construction on the same verse, taking the argument to be that among men there may be oppression but not with an almighty and just judge, so that the right course is to wait: men may indeed complain of an earthly tyrant, but how canst thou say thou beholdest him not?

Who it is that gives songs in the night, and who it is that asks after God, are both genuinely unsettled. Ellicott lays out the alternative without choosing hastily. Some render it so that the one who gives songs in the night is the selfish and luxurious oppressor who spends the night in feasting and revelry and never asks where God his Maker is, which Ellicott grants is an intelligible meaning; and though the phrase has become proverbial, and is very beautiful taken of God, it may be doubted whether that is so natural here, a matter he leaves to individual taste and judgment. The decision partly depends, he adds, on whether the question itself belongs to the cry of the oppressed or is Elihu's own, and he thinks on balance it is better to regard it as Elihu's. Clarke keeps the devotional reading but reports four others besides: the Chaldee has the high angels giving praise in the night, the Greek has God setting the night watches, the Syriac and Arabic have him giving meditations in the night, and Coverdale has him shining upon us that we might praise him in the night. Delitzsch renders the cry itself as a call for help by reason of the arm of the great, with no one saying where is my Creator, who gives songs of praise in the night.

On the comparison with the beasts both Henry and Clarke press the same reproach. Clarke cites the ox that knows his owner and the ass his master's crib while Israel does not know, and says that quadrupeds, reptiles and fowls have more gratitude to their masters than man has to his God. Henry makes it an argument rather than an exclamation: the greatest excellency of reason is that it makes us capable of religion, so that the oppressed who only cry under the arm of the mighty and never look up do no more than the brutes, which also complain when hurt. Ellicott reads the verse the other way about, that the oppression is so severe its victims forget God can give songs in the night. For the final denial Gill offers three senses of the vanity God will not hear, as a lie, as what is uttered rashly in a passionate and revengeful spirit, and as empty prayers for outward mercies only; while Ellicott notes that some take the whole clause as still part of the cry, so that it is the sufferers who say it is all in vain and God does not hear.
14:
What Job meant by saying he should not see God is read three ways, and the differences matter for whether Elihu's reproof lands. Henry takes it doubly, as a complaint that Job did not understand the meaning of God's severe dealings and could not discern their drift and design, and as a despair of ever seeing God's gracious returns, of seeing better days again; and he glosses the mood with the observation that as in prosperity we think our mountain will never be brought low, so in adversity we think our valley will never be filled, which is as absurd as to think, when the weather is either fair or foul, that it will always be so, that the flowing tide will always flow or the ebbing tide always ebb. Gill narrows it. God is invisible in his nature, yet Job had seen him in his works and trusted him as his salvation and had a full persuasion of the beatific vision; so the complaint cannot be about any of those, but only about not seeing God on a throne of judgment, hearing and trying his cause and acquitting him, which Job had often desired and despaired of ever seeing. Clarke and Ellicott approach it textually instead. Clarke notes that several manuscripts read thou shalt not see me and the Greek thou shalt not see us, the unpointed consonants admitting either him or us; Ellicott simply prefers dost not behold him to the received rendering.

The fifteenth verse is where the chapter becomes genuinely obscure, and Ellicott says so outright. The Authorised Version refers the first clause to God and the second to Job; he would rather render it that what God's anger has visited upon Job is as nothing compared with his deserts, and that God has not regarded the great abundance of his sin, that is, has not visited it with anger. He sets two further renderings beside his own, both of which make the absence of judgment the thing that emboldens Job, and notes that the word he translates arrogance is found nowhere else and appears to mean abundance or superfluity. Of the renderings he thinks his own gives the better sense, but holds that the general bearing of the verse is apparent however it is rendered: Job is encouraged in his murmurings because God has dealt too leniently with him. Clarke lands in the same place by a shorter route, preferring but now, because he visiteth not in his anger, and drawing from it the maxim that because vengeance is not speedily executed on an evil work the hearts of the children of men are set in them to do iniquity, which he says is in effect the charge Elihu brings. Henry reads the clause the other way round, as meaning that because Job did not trust God, the affliction which came at first from love now has displeasure mixed with it.

Two notes of unusual candour close the chapter. Ellicott, having defended Elihu's renderings at length, allows that his reproaches must have been some of the heaviest Job had to bear, and adds that happily the judgment was not to be long deferred. Clarke goes further and turns the indictment on the whole book: however the charge of multiplying words without knowledge may apply to Job, it most certainly applies very strongly and generally to the words not only of Job's three friends but to those of Elihu himself, the contest being frequently a strife of words. Henry, who defends Elihu throughout, nonetheless declines to follow the three friends in condemning Job for a hypocrite, charging him only with speaking unadvisedly with his lips when his spirit was provoked, and observing that when any of us does so it is a mercy to be told of it.
